Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

[LLM] CVE-2022-0492 cgroup release_agent container escape — unshare + rdma mount + release_agent chain Exploitation High
Hunts the published exploit signature for CVE-2022-0492: a process inside a container invokes 'unshare' to create user/cgroup namespaces and then mounts the RDMA cgroup controller, with a command line referencing the cgroup 'release_agent' file. This is the exact behavioural chain documented by Aqua Security, Palo Alto Unit 42 and Sysdig for the CISA-KEV-listed Linux kernel container escape. Rationale: Anchored on the published Falco/Sysdig rule for CVE-2022-0492 (unshare + mount + rdma + release_agent) and the Aqua / Unit 42 exploit walkthrough that the article explicitly cites. Cross-checked Unit 42 (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/), Aqua Security blog, and Sysdig (https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig). The 'release_agent' string + 'rdma' cgroup controller combo is article-specific and not matched by generic LOLBin / privilege-escalation rules. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/ • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/cve-2022-0492 • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/
ATT&CKT1611 T1068 T1059.004

   or (ProcessCommandLine has "unshare" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)-[UrmC]+|--user|--mount|--cgroup")

title: CVE-2022-0492 cgroup release_agent Container Escape via unshare
id: 7b3e8c1d-6a4f-4e21-9b8d-1f2a5c3d9e10
description: Detects the published CVE-2022-0492 exploit chain where a process uses unshare to create user/cgroup namespaces and mounts the rdma cgroup controller with a command line referencing the cgroup release_agent file. Pattern from Aqua Security, Unit 42 and Sysdig writeups.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/
  - https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/
  - https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-active-attacks-exploiting-android-linux-bugs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1068
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - cve.2022.0492
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_unshare:
    Image|endswith: '/unshare'
  selection_chain:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'release_agent'
  selection_mount:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'mount'
      - 'rdma'
      - 'cgroup'
  condition: selection_unshare and (selection_chain or selection_mount)
falsepositives:
  - Container security research / pentesting
  - Kubernetes upgrade tooling that legitimately remounts cgroupfs
level: high
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE (@process.name:unshare OR @process.command_line:*unshare*) (@process.command_line:*release_agent* OR (@process.command_line:*rdma* AND @process.command_line:*cgroup*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\/unshare$/i OR CommandLine=/unshare/i)
| (CommandLine=/release_agent/i OR (CommandLine=/rdma/i AND CommandLine=/cgroup/i))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

[LLM] CVE-2022-0492 — Write to cgroup release_agent file inside /sys/fs/cgroup hierarchy Installation High
Detects creation or modification of a 'release_agent' file inside the cgroup filesystem — the terminal step of the CVE-2022-0492 container-escape chain where the attacker plants a command (executed as root on the host) into release_agent and triggers notify_on_release. Article cross-referenced Aqua Security + Unit 42 research on this exact primitive. Rationale: release_agent is a cgroups v1-specific primitive — there is almost no benign reason for non-runtime code to write to it. Anchored on the article's named function (cgroup_release_agent_write) plus the Unit 42 / Aqua exploit chain (https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/). Detects the terminal step of the exploit even if the attacker writes from a shell rather than unshare directly (covering UC1's blind spots). Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/ • https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/ • https://www.sysdig.com/blog/detecting-mitigating-cve-2022-0492-sysdig • https://book.hacktricks.wiki/en/linux-hardening/privilege-escalation/docker-security/docker-breakout-privilege-escalation/docker-release_agent-cgroups-escape.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1611/
ATT&CKT1611 T1574 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName == "release_agent"
| where FolderPath has "/sys/fs/cgroup/" or FolderPath has "/cgroup/"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("systemd", "kubelet", "containerd", "containerd-shim", "runc", "crun", "dockerd")
             and InitiatingProcessAccountName == "root")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where TargetFileName == "release_agent"
| where TargetFilePath has "/sys/fs/cgroup/" or TargetFilePath has "/cgroup/"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileWritten")
| where not (ActingProcessName has_any ("systemd", "kubelet", "containerd", "runc", "crun", "dockerd")
             and ActorUsername == "root")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, EventType
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CVE-2022-0492 cgroup release_agent File Write
id: 9f4a2c7e-3d8b-4c5a-a6f1-2e8d9b3c4f50
description: Detects creation or modification of a release_agent file inside the /sys/fs/cgroup hierarchy. This is the persistence/trigger primitive of the CVE-2022-0492 container escape — the file is invoked by the kernel as root on the host when notify_on_release fires.
references:
  - https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/cve-2022-0492-cgroups/
  - https://www.aquasec.com/blog/new-linux-kernel-vulnerability-escaping-containers-by-abusing-cgroups/
  - https://terenceli.github.io/%E6%8A%80%E6%9C%AF/2022/03/06/cve-2022-0492
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/cisa-warns-of-active-attacks-exploiting-android-linux-bugs/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.t1611
  - attack.t1574
  - attack.privilege_escalation
  - cve.2022.0492
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '/release_agent'
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '/sys/fs/cgroup/'
      - '/cgroup/'
  filter_runtime:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/systemd'
      - '/kubelet'
      - '/containerd'
      - '/containerd-shim'
      - '/runc'
      - '/crun'
      - '/dockerd'
  condition: selection and not filter_runtime
falsepositives:
  - Container runtime startup (filtered above)

Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

What 345 Days of Untested Exposure Looks Like at a Bank

BleepingComputer
2026-06-03 4 use cases 2 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

A two-week penetration test can leave roughly 345 days of real-world exposure unvalidated. Sprocket Security explores why continuous testing is becoming critical as attack surfaces constantly change. [...]

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

[LLM] Acer Wave 7 unauthenticated acer_cgi.log credential disclosure (CVE-2026-49200) Exploitation High
Hunts HTTP requests to the /acer_cgi.log endpoint on Acer Wave 7 mesh routers (admin URLs http://192.168.76.1 / http://acerconnect.com). This file is reachable without auth and contains cleartext web + Telnet credentials, so any GET to that exact path is the entire CVE-2026-49200 exploit primitive. Rationale: The article explicitly names acer_cgi.log as the unauthenticated file containing cleartext web + Telnet credentials (CVE-2026-49200). Pivoting on that exact URI substring catches every PoC and exploit attempt with effectively zero benign traffic since the file is not a normal user-facing resource. Cross-referenced with the admin endpoints 192.168.76.1 and acerconnect.com given in the article body to scope to actual Acer Wave 7 targets. No external corroboration searched — same-day vendor advisory referenced in article body.

[LLM] Acer Wave 7 upload.cgi backup tamper for persistent backdoor (CVE-2026-49201) Installation Medium
Hunts POST requests to /upload.cgi on Acer Wave 7 routers carrying re-encrypted system backups. CVE-2026-49201 leaks a hardcoded AES key in upload.cgi that lets an attacker decrypt, modify (inject backdoor) and re-encrypt a backup so the device persists the implant on restore. Suspicious-shape POSTs to that endpoint from non-admin sources are the only on-wire artefact of the exploit. Rationale: Article identifies upload.cgi as the backup-processing binary holding the hardcoded AES key (CVE-2026-49201). POST is the only HTTP method consistent with the documented backup upload/restore action; pairing path + method + admin-destination (192.168.76.1 / acerconnect.com) tightens to the actual exploit primitive. Bytes-in floor (>1024) screens out probing or empty form submissions. Falcon and CloudWatch left empty — Falcon FDR doesn't carry HTTP URL paths, and the telemetry is web/network not AWS-native.
ATT&CKT1601.002 T1554 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has "upload.cgi"
   or (RemoteUrl has_any ("acerconnect.com", "192.168.76.1") and AdditionalFields has "upload.cgi")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountDomain,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(RequestURL)
| where RequestURL has "upload.cgi"
| where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
| extend BackupBytes = toint(ReceivedBytes)
| extend AdminTarget = iff(DestinationIP == "192.168.76.1" or DestinationHostName has "acerconnect.com", "acer-admin", "other")
| where AdminTarget == "acer-admin" or BackupBytes > 1024
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName,
          RequestURL, RequestMethod, BackupBytes, SentBytes, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct,
          RequestClientApplication, AdminTarget
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] HTTP/2 Bomb inbound exploitation: zero-window slow-hold against NGINX/Apache/IIS/Envoy/Pingora Exploitation Medium
Hunts the HTTP/2 Bomb attack pattern: a small number of source IPs opening long-lived HTTP/2 (h2/h2c) sessions to a web server on 80/443/8080/8443 while sending unusually low inbound bytes — the signature of a HEADERS-frame storm paired with a zero-byte INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE / 1-byte WINDOW_UPDATE drip that pins HPACK per-entry allocations indefinitely. Article-specific anchor: low-bandwidth source (~100 Mbps), seconds-to-minutes hold, single source can pin 32 GB on Apache HTTPD/Envoy in ~20s. Rationale: Anchors on Calif's HTTP/2 Bomb mechanics described in the article: low-bandwidth source pinning a server for >20s with many cheap requests yielding minimal bytes-in and zero/near-zero bytes-out (because the zero-window hold prevents response DATA frames). The vulnerable-process list (nginx/httpd/w3wp/envoy/pingora) matches the named affected stacks. Cross-checked with the Calif blog post and oss-sec disclosure. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/06/03/3 • https://github.com/califio/publications/blob/main/MADBugs/http2-bomb/nginx/README.md
ATT&CKT1190 T1499.003 T1499.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1h)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe","caddy.exe")
| where LocalPort in (80,443,8080,8443)
| summarize ConnCount=count(), DistinctSrcPorts=dcount(RemotePort), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, LocalPort
| extend WindowSec = datetime_diff('second', LastSeen, FirstSeen)
| where ConnCount > 100 and DistinctSrcPorts > 50 and WindowSec > 120
| order by ConnCount desc
let win = 5m;
let IISsig = W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where sPort in (80,443,8080,8443)
    | summarize ReqCount=count(), AvgCsBytes=avg(toint(csBytes)), MaxTimeTaken=max(toint(TimeTaken)) by cIP, Computer, sSiteName, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
    | where ReqCount > 300 and AvgCsBytes < 500 and MaxTimeTaken > 10000
    | extend Source="IIS";
let WAFsig = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
    | where DeviceVendor in ("F5","Imperva","Cloudflare","Akamai","Citrix","Fortinet")
    | where ApplicationProtocol has_any ("http2","h2","h2c")
    | summarize ReqCount=count(), TotalRecvBytes=sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)), DistinctSrcPorts=dcount(SourcePort) by SourceIP, DestinationHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
    | where ReqCount > 200 and TotalRecvBytes < 200000 and DistinctSrcPorts > 25
    | extend Source="WAF";
union IISsig, WAFsig
| order by TimeGenerated desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:iis OR source:envoy) @http.version:("HTTP/2.0" OR "HTTP/2" OR "h2" OR "h2c") @network.bytes_read:<500
#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 ConnectionDirection=1
| ContextImageFileName=/(nginx|httpd|w3wp|envoy|pingora|caddy)\.exe$/i
| LocalPort=/^(80|443|8080|8443)$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RemoteAddressIP4, ContextImageFileName], function=[count(as=conns), min(_time, as=first), max(_time, as=last)])
| window_sec := last - first
| conns > 100 AND window_sec > 120

[LLM] Web server process OOM/crash-restart cycle (HTTP/2 Bomb impact) Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream impact of HTTP/2 Bomb: nginx/httpd/w3wp/envoy worker processes repeatedly crashing and being restarted by services.exe/WerFault.exe within a short window, consistent with memory exhaustion (the article notes ~32 GB pinned in 20s on Apache/Envoy). Catches the attack from the endpoint side when perimeter telemetry is missing. Rationale: The article specifies that a single client can pin 32 GB of memory on Apache HTTPD and Envoy in ~20 seconds, leading to worker exhaustion / OOM kills. On Windows hosts and Linux hosts forwarding to Defender via MDE-for-Linux, the post-OOM symptom is a tight cluster of service-manager-initiated restarts of the web-server binary — far more frequent than any normal config-reload cadence. Cross-checked with the Calif disclosure where the PoC explicitly demonstrates 20s-to-OOM behaviour. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.calif.io/p/codex-discovered-a-hidden-http2-bomb • https://cybersecuritynews.com/http-2-bomb-remote-dos-exploit/
ATT&CKT1499.003 T1499.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where FileName in~ ("nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("services.exe","WerFault.exe","svchost.exe")
| summarize Restarts=count(), FirstRestart=min(Timestamp), LastRestart=max(Timestamp), Parents=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName) by DeviceName, FileName, bin(Timestamp, 30m)
| where Restarts >= 4
| extend WindowMin = datetime_diff('minute', LastRestart, FirstRestart)
| order by Restarts desc
let win = 30m;
let ProcRestarts = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | extend img = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
    | extend parent = tolower(tostring(split(ParentProcessName, "\\")[-1]))
    | where img in ("nginx.exe","httpd.exe","w3wp.exe","envoy.exe","pingora.exe")
    | where parent in ("services.exe","werfault.exe","svchost.exe")
    | summarize Restarts=count(), FirstRestart=min(TimeGenerated), LastRestart=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, img, bin(TimeGenerated, win)
    | where Restarts >= 4;
let SvcCrashes = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
    | where EventLog == "System" and EventID == 7034
    | where ParameterXml has_any ("nginx","httpd","Apache","W3SVC","envoy","pingora")
    | summarize Crashes=count(), LastCrash=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, win);
ProcRestarts | join kind=leftouter SvcCrashes on Computer | order by Restarts desc

[LLM] Windows Search URI NTLMv2 hash leak via search:crumb=location UNC handler Delivery High
Hunts the unpatched Windows search: URI abuse described in the article title: a search: URI carrying crumb=location:\\<attacker>\share is invoked (via cmd.exe `start`, shortcut, malicious HTML, or Office doc), causing the Search shell handler to reach the attacker's SMB share and leak the user's NTLMv2 hash before any error dialog renders. Anchor strings from the article code block: `search:query=` paired with `crumb=location:\\`. Rationale: Exact-string anchor from the article's code block: `start "" "search:query=test&crumb=location:\\10.0.1.100\share"`. The pair `search:` + `crumb=location:` together is the specific abuse pattern — neither token alone triggers the SMB fetch. Cross-checked with Huntress's deeper write-up confirming the handler resolves crumb=location even when filePath is absent, which is what makes this the NTLMv2-leak variant of CVE-2026-33829. Endpoint side is high-fidelity because no Microsoft-shipped tooling uses this combination. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/unpatched-ntlm-leak-windows-search-uri-handler • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/unpatched-windows-search-uri.html
ATT&CKT1187 T1557.001 T1204.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
let SearchUriCmd = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "search:" and ProcessCommandLine has "crumb=location:"
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, ReportId;
let SuspectSmbEgress = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where RemotePort in (445, 139)
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","SearchApp.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","SearchHost.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","outlook.exe","winword.exe","excel.exe")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemotePort;
union SearchUriCmd, SuspectSmbEgress
| order by Timestamp desc
let CmdHits = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where CommandLine has "search:" and CommandLine has "crumb=location:"
    | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine;
let SmbEgress = CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where DestinationPort in (445, 139)
    | where DeviceAction !in ("deny","block","drop")
    | where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DeviceName, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, ProcessName=SourceProcessName;
union CmdHits, SmbEgress
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Windows Search URI NTLMv2 Hash Leak via search:crumb=location UNC
id: 8c7f4d2a-1e9b-4a6f-b1d4-7e2f9c8d3a5b
description: Detects invocation of the Windows search: URI handler with a crumb=location parameter pointing at a UNC path, causing the Search shell handler to authenticate to the remote SMB share and leak the user's NTLMv2 hash. Unpatched at time of writing (Huntress disclosure, no CVE).
references:
  - https://www.huntress.com/blog/unpatched-ntlm-leak-windows-search-uri-handler
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/unpatched-windows-search-uri.html
author: detection-engineering
date: 2026/06/03
tags:
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1187
  - attack.t1557.001
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'search:'
      - 'crumb=location:'
  filter_machine:
    User|endswith: '$'
  condition: selection and not filter_machine
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate use of Windows Search saved-search URIs pointing at internal file shares (rare; should still be reviewed)
level: high
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @CommandLine:(*search\:* AND *crumb=location\:*) -@User:*$
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| regex("search:", field=CommandLine)
| regex("crumb=location:", field=CommandLine)
| NOT UserName=/\$$/
| table([_time, aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine])
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count, values(Processes.user) as user, values(Processes.process) as cmdline, values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent, min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*search:*" AND Processes.process="*crumb=location:*" by Processes.dest, Processes.process_name, _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort 0 - first_seen
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(Processes.user) as user, values(Processes.process) as cmdline, values(Processes.parent_process_name) as parent, min(_time) as first_seen from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process="*search:*" AND Processes.process="*crumb=location:*" by Processes.dest, Processes.process_name, _time span=1m | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | sort 0 - first_seen

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user

[LLM] Argamal COM Hijack of Windows Color System Calibration Loader CLSID Installation High
Detects HKCU CLSID hijack of the Windows Color System Calibration Loader {B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD} or the Stage1 staging CLSID {722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876} where InprocServer32 / ShellFolder points to a DLL in AppData\Local. This is Argamal's login-trigger persistence anchor. Rationale: Anchored on the two exact CLSIDs from the article ({B210D694-...} Calibration Loader and {722D0F89-...} Stage1 staging) plus the HKCU AppData\Local InprocServer32 payload location — the combination is article-specific and not produced by any legitimate Color System software (which writes HKLM).
ATT&CKT1546.015 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has_any ("{B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD}","{722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876}")
| where RegistryKey has "InprocServer32" or RegistryValueName =~ "ShellFolder"
| where RegistryValueData has "AppData\\Local" and RegistryValueData endswith ".dll"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has_any ("{B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD}","{722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876}")
| where (RegistryKey has "InprocServer32") or (RegistryValue =~ "ShellFolder")
| where RegistryValueData has "AppData\\Local" and RegistryValueData endswith ".dll"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
title: Argamal COM Hijack of Windows Color System Calibration Loader CLSID
id: 8b1ee0c8-9c1f-4e22-9b1a-1f6c1f9e9c01
description: Detects HKCU CLSID hijack of the Calibration Loader or Argamal Stage1 staging CLSID with InprocServer32 / ShellFolder pointing to an AppData\Local DLL.
references:

author: SOC
date: 2026/06/03
tags:

  - attack.defense_evasion

logsource:
  category: registry_event

    TargetObject|contains:
      - '{B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD}'

  subkey:
    TargetObject|contains:
      - '\InprocServer32'
      - '\ShellFolder'

    Details|contains: '\AppData\Local\'
    Details|endswith: '.dll'
  condition: clsid and subkey and appdata_dll
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:13 @TargetObject:(*B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD* OR *b210d694-c8df-490d-9576-9e20cdbc20bd* OR *722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876* OR *722d0f89-b69c-4700-ae8c-4a44350e4876*) @TargetObject:(*\\InprocServer32* OR *\\inprocserver32* OR *\\ShellFolder* OR *\\shellfolder*) @Details:(*\\AppData\\Local\\* OR *\\appdata\\local\\*)
#event_simpleName=AsepValueUpdate
| RegObjectName=/\{(B210D694-C8DF-490D-9576-9E20CDBC20BD|722D0F89-B69C-4700-AE8C-4A44350E4876)\}/i
| RegObjectName=/(InprocServer32|ShellFolder)/i
| RegStringValue=/\\AppData\\Local\\.+\.dll$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, RegObjectName, RegValueName, RegStringValue, ContextImageFileName], function=count())

| `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)`

[LLM] Argamal MI_V / MI_V2 Environment Variable Stage Handoff Installation High
Detects creation of the HKCU\Environment\MI_V or MI_V2 value used by Argamal Stage1 PowerShell to hand off the Base64-encoded Stage2 payload to a delayed scheduled task. The variable name is unique to this family. Rationale: MI_V / MI_V2 is a unique-to-Argamal env-var name documented in the Securelist write-up as the Stage1→Stage2 handoff. Anchored on the exact HKCU\Environment subkey + literal value names — no legitimate software writes these names.
ATT&CKT1140 T1546.015 T1027.013
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\Environment"
| where RegistryValueName in~ ("MI_V","MI_V2")
| extend ValueLen = strlen(tostring(RegistryValueData))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, ValueLen, RegistryValueDataPreview = substring(tostring(RegistryValueData),0,160), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey endswith "\\Environment"
| where RegistryValue in~ ("MI_V","MI_V2")
| extend ValueLen = strlen(tostring(RegistryValueData))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, ValueLen, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

[LLM] Argamal Stage2 BITSAdmin Pull of zaesdl.dat from GitHub Command & Control High
Detects bitsadmin.exe invoked with /transfer (or /addfile + /resume) downloading the AES-encrypted RAT payload named zaesdl.dat — Argamal's Stage2 retrieval pattern using GitHub-hosted infrastructure. Rationale: Anchored on the exact payload filename (zaesdl.dat) and Argamal's documented use of GitHub-hosted Stage2 retrieved via bitsadmin. The combination of bitsadmin + github + .dat extension is extremely uncommon outside this family.

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\bitsadmin.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/transfer","/addfile","/create","/resume")
| where CommandLine has_any ("zaesdl.dat","raw.githubusercontent.com","github.com","gist.githubusercontent.com")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Detects connections to the Argamal RAT C2 infrastructure: hardcoded IP 186.158.223.35, the three dyndns FQDNs (asper1.freeddns.org, winst0.kozow.com, country1.ignorelist.com), and the malware's unusual UDP/57441 heartbeat / TCP/3747 extended-mode / UDP/63559 payload-update ports. Rationale: Hardcoded IP 186.158.223.35 plus three named dyndns FQDNs and the three unusual ports (UDP/57441 heartbeat, TCP/3747 extended-mode, UDP/63559 payload-update) are pulled verbatim from the Securelist IOC section. The port-only branch is gated by AppData\Local origin to suppress unrelated egress.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1095 T1568.002 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteIP == "186.158.223.35")
    or (RemoteUrl in~ ("asper1.freeddns.org","winst0.kozow.com","country1.ignorelist.com"))
    or (RemotePort in (57441,3747,63559) and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "AppData\\Local")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where (DstIpAddr == "186.158.223.35")
    or (DstHostname in~ ("asper1.freeddns.org","winst0.kozow.com","country1.ignorelist.com"))
    or (DstPortNumber in (57441,3747,63559))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes

[LLM] Argamal Scheduled Task Pointing at AppData\Local DLL via Color System Calibration Loader Installation Medium
Detects scheduled task creation/modification where the Argamal Stage1 PowerShell registers a delayed (3-day) trigger or repurposes the \Microsoft\Windows\WindowsColorSystem\Calibration Loader task to launch a random-named DLL from %USER%\AppData\Local. Catches the persistence and the delayed-detonation primitives in one shot. Rationale: References the exact task path \Microsoft\Windows\WindowsColorSystem\Calibration Loader, the MI_V env-var fed to Stage2, and the AppData\Local DLL target — all article-specific. Catches both the 3-day-delayed task primitive and the recurring login-trigger task in one rule.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1546.015 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Calibration Loader","WindowsColorSystem","MI_V")
   or (ProcessCommandLine has "AppData\\Local" and ProcessCommandLine has ".dll" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rundll32","regsvr32","-Command","-EncodedCommand"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\schtasks.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith_cs "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create","/change","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Calibration Loader","WindowsColorSystem","MI_V")
   or (CommandLine has "AppData\\Local" and CommandLine has ".dll")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: Argamal Stage1 Scheduled Task Targeting AppData DLL or Color System Calibration Loader

detection:

| ImageFileName=/\\(schtasks|powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i

[LLM] Argamal Loader Artifacts — natives2_blob.bin / Modified ffmpeg.dll IOC Sweep Installation High
Detects the Argamal loader files on disk: the natives2_blob.bin script-executor DLL by filename, the known modified ffmpeg.dll by SHA1 (42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85), and the script-executor DLL by SHA1 (edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d). Triggers on file write, file open, or image load. Rationale: Hash IOC sweep + named-artifact hunt. The filename natives2_blob.bin is unique to Argamal (does not appear in any legitimate ffmpeg / game shipment) and the two SHA1s are confirmed-malicious per the Kaspersky write-up. Union across DeviceFileEvents and DeviceImageLoadEvents catches both the drop and the load.
ATT&CKT1574.001 T1204.002 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
union
  (DeviceFileEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where FileName =~ "natives2_blob.bin" or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="FileEvent", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where FileName =~ "ffmpeg.dll" and SHA1 == "42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ImageLoad", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceImageLoadEvents | where Timestamp > ago(90d) | where SHA1 == "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="ImageLoad", ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, SHA1, FileOriginUrl="", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "natives2_blob.bin"
    or TargetFileSHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85","edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA1, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or MD5 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or SHA1 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d") or MD5 in~ ("42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["42add9475e67a1ccc6a6af94b5475d3defc01b85", "edce72f59e4c1d136cd1946af70d334c19df858d"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

2026-06-03 19 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

The Minecraft-focused malware-as-a-service (MaaS) campaign has been codenamed Weedhack by McAfee Labs, stating the activity has been active since January 2026 and impersonates Minecraft clients and mods to infect users. [LLM] Weedhack DonutDupe.jar launched via java.exe (Minecraft MaaS first stage) Delivery High
Catches java.exe (or javaw.exe) executing the article's first-stage JAR 'DonutDupe.jar' dropped from a malicious Minecraft mod/client site. Article-specific binary + parent-child shape, distinct from generic javaw activity. Rationale: DonutDupe.jar is the named first-stage from McAfee's Weedhack writeup; java/javaw executing a file literally containing that string is extremely high-fidelity. Minecraft launchers normally invoke launcher-specific JARs (minecraft.jar, forge-*.jar), not files containing 'DonutDupe'. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","javaws.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "DonutDupe" and ProcessCommandLine has ".jar"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\java.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\javaw.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\javaws.exe"
| where CommandLine has "DonutDupe" and CommandLine has ".jar"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Weedhack C2 dashboard contact: outbound to weedhack[.]to Command & Control High
DNS or HTTP contact with weedhack[.]to, the clear-net dashboard that operators use to view stolen credentials and command Weedhack-infected hosts. Domain is the central operational artefact of the campaign. Rationale: weedhack[.]to is the only named domain in the McAfee writeup — it is the operator dashboard, so any resolution from an enterprise host is by-definition an infection. Single-IOC, single-event detection. Fixed Sentinel schema: switched from DeviceName (Defender-only) to Computer/ClientIP on DnsEvents, SrcHostname on ImDnsActivity/ImWebSession, and SourceHostName on CommonSecurityLog. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
union
( DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has "weedhack.to"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort ),
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where AdditionalFields has "weedhack.to"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, AdditionalFields )
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
( DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has "weedhack.to"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode ),
( ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has "weedhack.to"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DnsQuery, DnsResponseCodeName, DvcHostname ),
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has "weedhack.to" or DstHostname has "weedhack.to"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url, DvcHostname ),
( CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where RequestURL has "weedhack.to" or DestinationHostName has "weedhack.to"
  | project TimeGenerated, SourceHostName, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] Weedhack EtherHiding: java.exe contacts public Ethereum RPC endpoints Command & Control Medium
Detects Java processes (the Weedhack JAR chain) issuing JSON-RPC to public Ethereum nodes — the EtherHiding technique used to fetch the next-stage C2 server. Java reaching an Ethereum mainnet RPC is essentially never legitimate in an enterprise environment. Rationale: Article explicitly cites EtherHiding (Ethereum blockchain as dead-drop resolver) for the DonutDupe→C2 hop. Sentinel ASIM ImNetworkSession lacks process attribution, so we join SecurityEvent 4688 (java.exe spawns) to ImNetworkSession on Computer+30-minute window. Fixed prior schema error: removed ActingProcessName/ActingProcessCommandLine from ImNetworkSession (those are ImProcessCreate fields). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/
ATT&CKT1102 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","javaws.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any (EthRpc) or tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host) has_any (EthRpc)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

let EthNet = union isfuzzy=true

[LLM] Weedhack multi-stage JAR drops: Elevator/SecurityManager/Component.jar Installation High
File-create events for the three follow-on Weedhack JARs (Elevator.jar, SecurityManager.jar, Component.jar) written to disk after DonutDupe.jar runs. These exact names are stage-2/3/4 in the article's chain and are not legitimate Minecraft artefacts. Rationale: Article names these three JARs as Weedhack's stage-2 (Elevator), stage-3 persistence (SecurityManager), and stage-4 RAT (Component). The names 'SecurityManager.jar' and 'Component.jar' especially are deliberately innocuous-sounding but are not standard Minecraft / Forge / Fabric artefacts. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html

| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

[LLM] CountLoader: EXE → PowerShell → mshta.exe obfuscated JS chain Delivery High
Detects the CountLoader execution chain described in the article: an EXE launches a PowerShell command that downloads/executes an obfuscated JS loader via mshta.exe. Targets the three-process tree shape (EXE→powershell→mshta) that's distinctive vs ordinary mshta usage. Rationale: Article explicitly states 'The loader is executed using mshta.exe' and 'PowerShell command, which downloads and executes an obfuscated JavaScript loader'. The PowerShell→mshta parent→child relationship is the article-specific signature; mshta launched from cmd.exe/explorer.exe is normal-ish, but launched from powershell with a URL/javascript: arg is the CountLoader pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/005/
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.001 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(javascript:|vbscript:|http[s]?://|\.hta\b|new\s+ActiveXObject|WScript\.Shell)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(javascript:|vbscript:|http[s]?://|\.hta\b|new\s+ActiveXObject|WScript\.Shell)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

[LLM] CountLoader USB propagation: scripts/EXEs written to removable media Actions on Objectives Medium
Detects CountLoader's USB-spreading behaviour — writes of .js / .hta / .lnk / autorun.inf / .exe to removable drives by a process recently associated with the loader chain. Article attributes ~9,000 of the 86,000 CountLoader infections to USB spread. Rationale: Article specifies CountLoader 'attempts to spread via USB drives' and that ~9k of 86k infections came from USB/removable media. Combination of removable-drive root path + LNK/HTA/JS/autorun.inf + non-Explorer writer is the classic USB-worm shape and isolates from legitimate user file copies. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1091/
ATT&CKT1091 T1547.009
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"^[D-Z]:\\"
| where FileName =~ "autorun.inf" or FileName endswith ".lnk" or FileName endswith ".hta" or FileName endswith ".js" or FileName endswith ".vbs"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","GoogleDriveFS.exe")
| summarize FileCount=dcount(FileName), Files=make_set(FileName,20), SamplePath=any(FolderPath), arg_max(Timestamp,*) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, bin(Timestamp,5m)
| where FileCount >= 2
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileCreate","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"^[D-Z]:\\"
| where TargetFileName =~ "autorun.inf" or TargetFileExtension in~ ("lnk","hta","js","vbs")
| where ActingProcessName !endswith "\\explorer.exe" and ActingProcessName !endswith "\\OneDrive.exe"
| summarize FileCount=dcount(TargetFileName), Files=make_set(TargetFileName,20), arg_max(TimeGenerated,*) by DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, bin(TimeGenerated,5m)
| where FileCount >= 2
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(D\:\\* OR E\:\\* OR F\:\\* OR G\:\\* OR H\:\\*) @TargetFilename:(*autorun.inf OR *.lnk OR *.hta OR *.js OR *.vbs) -@Image:(*\explorer.exe OR *\OneDrive.exe OR *\Dropbox.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^[D-Z]:\\/i TargetFileName=/(autorun\.inf|\.lnk|\.hta|\.js|\.vbs)$/i
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(explorer|OneDrive|Dropbox)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())
| count > 1

[LLM] Pirated-miner DLL side-load via HLS Installer.874.exe Installation High
Detects the article's miner-delivery vector: legitimate 'HLS Installer.874.exe' loading a non-Microsoft DLL from its working directory — the side-loading mechanism that injects the SilentCryptoMiner-fork loader. Tracks both the process launch and the suspicious image load. Rationale: Kaspersky's writeup (cited in article) names exactly 'HLS Installer.874.exe' as the legitimate side-load host for the SilentCryptoMiner fork. The filename is too specific to occur by chance; any execution from a host that touched a pirated-streaming site should be treated as the miner installer. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/weedhack-attacks-minecraft-users.html
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1496
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
let HlsProcs = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where FileName =~ "HLS Installer.874.exe"
    | project ProcTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, ProcessId, FolderPath, AccountName, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine;
let SideLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(90d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "HLS Installer.874.exe"
    | where FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Windows\\" and FolderPath !startswith "C:\\Program Files\\"
    | where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName != "Microsoft Corporation"
    | project LoadTime=Timestamp, DeviceName, LoadedDll=FileName, LoadedPath=FolderPath, LoadedSHA256=SHA256, InitiatingProcessId;
HlsProcs
| union SideLoads
| order by coalesce(ProcTime, LoadTime) desc
union isfuzzy=true
( SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "HLS Installer.874.exe" or CommandLine has "HLS Installer.874.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName ),
( ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(90d)
  | where ActingProcessName endswith "HLS Installer.874.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "HLS Installer.874.exe"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
